name: Reversi
intro: Learn Reversi (Othello) in minutes: trapping and flipping, passing and scoring, then the strategy that wins: corners, danger squares, quiet moves and stable discs.

units.name: How Reversi works
units.blurb: Flipping, passing and how the game is scored.

lessons.title: How to play Reversi: the rules
lessons.summary: Reversi (Othello) in one minute: place a disc to trap your opponent’s discs in a line and flip them to your colour. Learn by playing.
lessons.wrap: Trap a line, flip it. Next: flipping lots of discs at once.

steps.text: Reversi, also sold as Othello, is played on an 8×8 board. You have the gold discs and your opponent has black. The game starts with two of each in the middle, and gold moves first.

On your turn you place one disc so that it traps a line of your opponent’s discs between it and another of your discs. Every trapped disc flips to your colour.

Watch gold trap one black disc.
A move is only allowed if it flips at least one disc. Here, gold has exactly four allowed moves.
steps.prompt: Tap every square where gold can play.
steps.wrong: That square doesn’t trap a black disc between it and a gold one.
steps.done: All four. Each one traps a single black disc.

steps.text: Your turn for real. The dots show where you can play.
steps.prompt: Make any move and watch the flip.
steps.done: Flipped. That disc is gold now, until black flips it back.

lessons.title: Reversi flipping: lines and two directions
lessons.summary: In Reversi one disc can flip a whole line, and lines in several directions at once. Practise finding the moves that flip the most.
lessons.wrap: Look along all eight directions from the square you play. Next: passing and how the game ends.

steps.text: Every disc in the trapped line flips, however long the line is.
steps.prompt: Flip all three black discs in the row at once.
steps.wrong: Look along the row of three black discs. Where does a gold disc trap the whole row?

steps.text: A single move can trap lines in several directions: across, up and down, and diagonally. All of them flip.
steps.prompt: Find the move that flips four discs, in two directions.
steps.wrong: Try each empty square next to a black disc and look in every direction, not just along the row.
steps.done: Three across and one on the diagonal.

steps.text: One more rule.
steps.prompt: Do discs flip if they’re trapped by a chain reaction, after the first flips?
options: No, only the lines your new disc traps
steps.explain: No. Only the lines between your new disc and your other discs flip. There’s no chain reaction.

lessons.title: Reversi passing, the end of the game and scoring
lessons.summary: What happens in Reversi when you can’t move, how the game ends, and how the winner is decided by counting discs.
lessons.wrap: Pass when you must, count at the end. Next: a quick rules check.

steps.text:
If you have no move that flips a disc, you pass and your opponent goes again. If you do have a move, you must play one.

The game ends when neither player can move, usually because the board is full. Then you count: most discs wins.
Quick checks.
steps.prompt: You have no move that flips anything. What happens?
options: You pass, and your opponent moves again
steps.explain: You pass. The game only ends when neither player can move.

steps.text: The board is full: 37 gold discs and 27 black.
steps.explain: Gold, with more discs. 32 each would be a draw.

units.name: Rules check
units.blurb: Show you know the rules, then on to strategy.

lessons.title: Reversi rules check
lessons.summary: A quick Reversi rules check: flip a line, then answer two questions about passing and the end of the game. Pass it to unlock strategy.
lessons.wrap: Rules done. Now for strategy, starting with the most valuable squares on the board.

steps.text: Three questions. First, a move.
steps.prompt: Make the move that flips the most discs.

steps.text: Second.
steps.prompt: Can you play a disc that doesn’t flip anything?
options: No, every move must flip at least one disc
steps.explain: No. If no move flips a disc, you pass instead.

steps.text: Last one.
steps.explain: When neither player can move, usually because the board is full.

units.name: Winning ideas
units.blurb: Corners, danger squares, mobility and stable discs.

lessons.title: Reversi strategy: take the corners
lessons.summary: Corners are the most valuable squares in Reversi: a disc there can never be flipped. Learn why, and practise grabbing one.
lessons.wrap: A corner is yours for good. Next: the squares that give corners away.

steps.text:
A disc in a corner can never be flipped: there’s no square beyond it to trap it from.

Corners are also anchors. Discs along the edges next to your corner become hard to flip too.
Black has left a corner open for you.
steps.wrong: Look at the four corners of the board. One of them traps a black diagonal.
steps.done: Yours for the rest of the game.

steps.text: Check the idea.
steps.prompt: Can your corner disc ever be flipped back?
steps.explain: Never. Nothing can be placed beyond a corner, so it can’t be trapped.

lessons.title: Reversi danger squares: X-squares and C-squares
lessons.summary: The squares next to an empty corner are dangerous in Reversi. Learn the X-squares and C-squares, and how playing there hands over a corner.
lessons.wrap: Stay off the squares next to an empty corner. Next: why flipping fewer discs is often better.

steps.text:
The squares diagonally next to a corner are called X-squares (red). The edge squares beside a corner are C-squares (marked with dots).

While the corner is empty, playing on them often lets your opponent take the corner.
Watch: gold plays on the X-square, and black jumps straight into the corner.
Same position, your move.
steps.prompt: Make any move that doesn’t give away a corner.
steps.wrong: That’s the X-square: black takes the corner next. Pick another square.
steps.done: Good. The corner stays closed to black.

lessons.title: Reversi strategy: quiet moves and mobility
lessons.summary: Flipping lots of discs early in Reversi often backfires. Learn quiet moves that leave your opponent few good options.
lessons.wrap: Fewer discs, fewer choices for them. Next: discs that are safe forever.

steps.text:
Beginners flip as many discs as they can. Strong players usually do the opposite in the opening and middle game.

Every move you make should leave your opponent as few good moves as possible. This is called mobility. Run your opponent out of safe moves and they’ll be forced onto the danger squares.
Think about it.
steps.prompt: Early in the game, why can having fewer discs be good?
options: It isn’t: more discs always wins
Your opponent has fewer of your discs to trap, so fewer moves
Fewer discs means you move twice
steps.explain: Every gold disc on the edge of the group gives black something to trap. Fewer discs means fewer black options.

steps.text: Every move here flips one disc, but they leave black very different choices. Most leave black 7 to 9 moves.
steps.prompt: Find the quiet move that leaves black only four replies.
steps.wrong: That one leaves black lots of options. Look for a move that tucks in next to your own discs.
steps.done: Black has just four moves now, and one of them is an X-square black would rather not touch.

lessons.title: Reversi stable discs: the edges and corners
lessons.summary: Stable discs in Reversi can never be flipped. Learn how a corner makes the edge discs next to it safe, and count your stable discs.
lessons.wrap: Corners, then the edges they anchor. That’s the Reversi path complete!

steps.text:
A disc that can never be flipped is called stable. The corner is the first stable disc.

Discs on the edge, in an unbroken line from your corner, are stable too: nothing can get behind them.
Gold has the top-left corner and some discs along the two edges beside it.
steps.prompt: Tap every gold disc that can never be flipped.
steps.wrong: That disc could still be trapped. Stick to the corner and the edge discs joined to it.
steps.done: All four: the corner and the edge discs joined to it.

steps.text: Last question.
steps.prompt: At the end of the game, what matters?
options: Who had more discs in the middle game
Who has more discs when the board is full
steps.explain: Only the final count matters. Corners, stable discs and mobility are how you make sure it’s yours.
